# The vocabulary of event power.

> P17, Powerlock, MDB, diversity factor, stand-to-stand feeding, Twin generator sets, HVO, Stage V: the terms of event power explained simply.

Source: https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/glossary/ · Dark Side Energy · Updated: 2026-10-06

Distribution cabinets, connectors, protection devices, energy: the terms you will come across in our quotes, on our plans and on site, explained simply.

- **Distribution cabinet (armoire de distribution)**: Mobile electrical assembly that takes a high-current incoming supply, for example 125 A or 400 A, and splits it into protected outgoing circuits, for example 16 A, 32 A or 63 A, feeding the distribution boxes and equipment.
- **Power assessment (bilan de puissance)**: Inventory of all the electrical equipment at an event, with each item's power, connection type and diversity factor. It is used to size the sources, cables and protection devices.
- **Voltage drop (chute de tension)**: Drop in voltage along a cable, caused by its resistance. It increases with length and current, and decreases as the cross-section increases. The French standard NF C 15-100 limits it to 3% for lighting and 5% for other uses on an installation supplied from the public low-voltage grid.
- **Stand power box (coffret de stand)**: Small distribution board that supplies a single stand at a trade show or exhibition. It is fitted with a 30 mA RCD to protect people.
- **Temporary metered connection (compteur forain)**: Temporary connection to the public distribution grid, with metering, used to supply a temporary event such as a fair, a market or a festival.
- **Power factor, cos φ (facteur de puissance)**: Ratio of active power, in watts, to apparent power, in volt-amperes. It equals 1 for a purely resistive load and is lower for motors or some electronic power supplies.
- **30 mA RCD (différentiel 30 mA)**: Device that cuts the circuit when it detects a leakage current of 30 mA, for example through a person's body. It is what protects people against electrocution.
- **Circuit breaker (disjoncteur)**: Protective device that cuts a circuit when the current exceeds its rating (overload) or in the event of a short circuit. Its breaking capacity is expressed in kiloamperes (kA).
- **Diversity factor (foisonnement)**: Coefficient between 0 and 1 that reflects the fact that not all appliances run at full power at the same time. A realistic diversity factor avoids oversizing the installation.
- **Generator (groupe électrogène)**: Combustion engine that drives an alternator to produce electricity. Control electronics keep the voltage and frequency stable.
- **Twin zero-interruption generator set (groupe Twin zéro coupure)**: Two synchronised generators, each supplying 50% of the load. If one fails, the other takes over the whole load without interruption. Configurations with 3 or 4 synchronised generators also exist.
- **Generator technician (GroupMan)**: Technician in charge of monitoring and operating the generators during an event.
- **HVO**: Renewable fuel made from hydrotreated oils and fats (Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil), which can be used instead of diesel in compatible generators.
- **Stand-to-stand feeding (ilotage)**: Powering a stand from another stand's box. It is systematically refused by trade show safety officers, because it prevents the RCD protection from doing its job properly.
- **kVA and kW**: The kW measures active power, the power actually consumed. The kVA measures apparent power, which determines the size of cables, protection devices and sources. Active power = apparent power × cos φ.
- **Single-phase and three-phase (monophasé et triphasé)**: On a 230/400 V network, single-phase supplies 230 V between a phase and the neutral. Three-phase supplies 400 V between phases and carries more power for the same current.
- **P17**: Name commonly used in France for industrial sockets and plugs complying with the CEI 60309 standard (IEC 60309), in 16, 32, 63 and 125 A, single-phase or three-phase. They are the standard for event power distribution.
- **Battery pack (pack batterie)**: Mobile energy storage that powers an event without a combustion engine, on its own or in a hybrid setup with a generator. Its power is expressed in kVA and its capacity in kWh, for example 90 kVA for 120 kWh.
- **Cable protector (passage de câbles)**: Floor-laid protection that channels and protects cables across circulation areas. Wheelchair-accessible ramps allow people with reduced mobility to cross them.
- **Powerlock**: High-power, single-pole locking connectors, one per phase, one for neutral and one for earth, used for links of 400 A and above between sources and distribution cabinets.
- **Pass-through outlet (recopie)**: Outlet on a distribution cabinet or box with the same rating as its incoming supply, used to feed another piece of equipment in cascade.
- **Single-line diagram (schéma unifilaire)**: Simplified representation of an electrical installation in which each link is drawn as a single line, from the source to the outgoing circuits, with the protection devices and ratings.
- **Cable size (section de câble)**: Cross-sectional area of a cable's conducting core, expressed in mm². It is chosen according to the current, the length, the installation method and the permissible voltage drop.
- **Stage V**: The most stringent level of the European regulation on emissions from non-road mobile machinery engines (Regulation (EU) 2016/1628), which applies in particular to mobile generators.
- **Blue and yellow tariffs (tarif bleu et tarif jaune)**: Former names of connections to the French low-voltage grid: *tarif bleu* up to 36 kVA, *tarif jaune* from 36 to 250 kVA.
- **Four-pole, 3P+N (tétra)**: Four-pole connection or distribution cabinet: three phases and a neutral, plus earth.
- **Main distribution board, MDB (TGBT)**: Main low-voltage board, at the origin of the installation, which receives the main supply and feeds the distribution cabinets.

# What is event power distribution?

> Event power distribution: starting from the venue's supplies to distribute electricity safely. And why taking power from the next stand is banned.

Source: https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/did-you-know/event-power-distribution/ · Dark Side Energy · Updated: 2026-10-06

8 May 2017 · 2 min read · Updated 6 October 2026

- Event power distribution starts from the venue's supplies and takes electricity wherever the organisers need it, in compliance with safety standards.
- For live shows, the distribution cabinets sit behind the stage, ideally with one source per department.
- At trade shows, every stand has its own distribution box with a 30 mA RCD: *ilotage* (sharing a supply between stands) is banned.

Dark Side Energy specialises in event power distribution. Fine, but what exactly does that mean?

Every event is unique, and so is its configuration. Halls and venues designed for events are equipped with one or more main power supplies.

Event power distribution therefore means starting from that supply, or those supplies, and distributing electricity to the places the organisers ask for, while complying with safety standards: the right [cable sizes](https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/did-you-know/cable-size/) for the voltage, current and length, the right protection for people, the right protection for power circuits, and so on.

To do this, we use distribution cabinets.

## In live entertainment

The distribution cabinets end up behind the stage and, ideally, each department has its own source, with its own cabinet or cabinets, to avoid “buzz” and other electrical interference caused by the electronics in some equipment.

## For trade shows, fairs and exhibitions

It is a completely different story. Every stand **must** have its own distribution box fitted with a 30 mA RCD (protection of people). If an exhibitor runs an extension lead from the neighbouring stand, this is called *ilotage*, and safety officers refuse it every time.

But why? For several reasons, but one is very simple to explain.

You have a faulty appliance with current leaking to its casing. You touch it and the current flows through your body: **the 30 mA RCD cuts the power instantly**.

If the box is not on your stand and also supplies the stand it sits on, it also cuts the power to that exhibitor, who, having seen no problem on their own stand, resets the RCD. If your hand is still on the appliance, you get a second jolt (at best…).

> So yes, when you visit a trade show with 300 stands, if those 300 exhibitors need electricity, there are 300 distribution boxes of every power rating at that show.

Need power distribution for your trade show or your stage?

[Our core business: power distribution](https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/power-distribution/)

[What is a Twin zero-interruption generator set?](https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/did-you-know/twin-generators/)

# What is a Twin zero-interruption generator set?

> Twin zero-interruption generator set: two synchronised generators, each carrying 50% of the load. If one fails, there is no interruption.

Source: https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/did-you-know/twin-generators/ · Dark Side Energy · Updated: 2026-10-06

8 May 2017 · 2 min read · Updated 6 October 2026

- A Twin zero-interruption generator set is two synchronised generators, each supplying 50% of the load.
- If one fails, the other takes over the whole load without any interruption.
- Computers and sound and lighting consoles do not notice a thing. You can go up to 3 or 4 synchronised generators.

Is your event in a remote location? Do you need more power than the building can give you? So you decide to hire a generator! Good, but why is the hire company offering you a Twin zero-interruption generator set?

## Let's start at the beginning

A generator is an engine running on fuel oil, diesel or GNR (French non-road diesel), which drives an alternator and so produces electricity.

No rocket science so far, except that, to keep the voltage and frequency stable, the whole thing is managed by an electronic board. Still with me?

Every hire company will sing the praises of its generators. It is still an engine, with all the vagaries of mechanics **and** electronics. The whole thing is very reliable and servicing is done before every hire (at least at our suppliers), but a breakdown can always happen: there is no such thing as zero risk, just like with your car.

## Enter the Twin zero-interruption generator set

Two generators connected together run at the same time: they synchronise and each supplies 50% of the load.

If one of the two generators fails, the other takes over the missing 50% and, as it is already running, there is **no interruption at all**: electronic equipment does not see the failure and does not shut down.

Indeed, a computer that suffers even a micro-interruption may well end up with a dead hard drive as a result. Some lighting or sound consoles run on an operating system that needs several seconds, or even several minutes, to restart after a power cut. Needless to say, some productions do not take that risk and therefore use this system.

**Bonus:** in certain more specific cases, you can even go up to 3 or 4 synchronised generators (tri-pack, quadri-pack).

Today we also offer Stage V generators in twin versions and battery packs, on their own or in hybrid setups.

[See available power sources](https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/equipment/#energie)

# Cable size depends on current, but also on length!

> Why cable size depends on current but also on length: resistance, heating and voltage drop, explained simply.

Source: https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/did-you-know/cable-size/ · Dark Side Energy · Updated: 2026-10-06

8 May 2017 · 1 min read · Updated 6 October 2026

- A cable is a very good conductor, but it is also a resistance.
- The longer it is, the more it heats up and the greater the voltage drop.
- Cable size is therefore chosen according to the current and according to the length.

The size of electrical cables is very (too) often overlooked.

In simple terms, voltage (in volts) pushes current (in amperes), held back by resistance (in ohms).

Plenty of calculations explain this, but the aim of these articles is to help you understand the basics of our trade in a simple way.

An electrical cable is made of copper or aluminium. These materials are very good conductors, but they are also resistances (small, but present).

The length of a cable increases its heating and causes a **voltage drop**.

Many devices have a fairly narrow acceptable voltage range: often 220 to 250 V. If a device receives less, it may not work properly, or may even fail.

Choosing the cable size is therefore important when running long lengths. There are many charts that let you choose easily, and our calculator does it for you.

Calculate the voltage drop on your line: cable size, length, current, single-phase or three-phase.

[Open the electrical calculator](https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/electrical-calculator/#chute-de-tension)

[What is a Twin zero-interruption generator set?](https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/did-you-know/twin-generators/)

# Why does it “trip”?

> Why a distribution box “trips”: 30 mA RCD and circuit breaker explained simply. Faulty appliance or overloaded circuit?

Source: https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/did-you-know/why-it-trips/ · Dark Side Energy · Updated: 2026-10-06

8 May 2017 · 1 min read · Updated 6 October 2026

- The 30 mA RCD cuts the power when an appliance leaks current: it protects people.
- The circuit breaker cuts the power in the event of an overload or a short circuit: it protects the installation.
- When it trips, the box has done its job: look for the faulty appliance or spread your appliances over several circuits.

I think the sentence I have heard most often in our trade is: “There's a problem with your box, it keeps tripping!”

Yes, for most clients, when “it trips”, it is the fault of the electrician or of their distribution box.

## Back to basics

A distribution box is fitted with two main protective devices:

- a **30 mA RCD**, which protects people against leakage current;
- one or more **circuit breakers**, which protect the circuits against a current higher than they can withstand.

So when an RCD has tripped, it means that one or more appliances plugged into the distribution box have a fault, often a current leakage problem. This fault, or these faults added together, exceed 30 mA, so the RCD cuts the power for safety.

The circuit breaker, for its part, trips as soon as the current flowing through it exceeds the current it is rated to let through (expressed in amperes). It also protects against short circuits (its breaking capacity is expressed in kiloamperes).

## To sum up

Either you have one or more faulty appliances, or you have plugged too many appliances into the same circuit.

> As for the box, it has either saved your life or saved your installation.

Check the power of your appliances before plugging them in.

[Run a power assessment](https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/power-assessment/)

[Cable size depends on current, but also on length!](https://www.darkside-energy.com/en/did-you-know/cable-size/)
